newsitem.title: USA: Republicans cautious on using CPI as budget tool.
newsitem.headline: Republicans cautious on using CPI as budget tool.

text.p: Republicans in Congress are shying away from using the Consumer Price Index as a tool to cut the budget deficit, though it had appeared that changes in the inflation gauge could be a magic fix for the budget.

Joint Economic Committee Chairman Jim Saxton, a Republican congressman from New Jersey, on Friday joined a growing list of senior lawmakers who are holding back from latching on to planned changes in the government's CPI as a way to reduce the deficit.

A congressional advisory commission in December reported that the CPI overstated increases in the cost of living by 1.1 percentage points a year. Reducing the CPI could cut the deficit by more than $600 billion over 10 years, the commission said in its report.
"I think it is fair to say that although there is a consensus that the CPI may overstate inflation, the extent of this overstatement is at least debatable," Saxton said at a hearing last week.
While lowering the CPI could wipe out a chunk of the deficit, it would be a politically difficult gesture because benefits for certain federal programmes would be reduced.
Increases in Social Security benefits, veterans benefits and federal pensions are pegged to the CPI, so lowering the index would mean less government spending in those areas.
Tax brackets, income tax deductions and exemptions are also tied to the index, and lowering the CPI could have the effect of higher taxes for some taxpayers.
"There would seem to be ample reason for Congress to examine this issue carefully before making any hasty decision with regard to it," Saxton said.

An analysis by the Joint Economic Committee showed that about 40 percent of the direct effects of legislative reductions in the CPI would comprise tax increases on middle-class taxpayers and the rest would affect entitlement beneficiaries, Saxton said.
"Congress should consider whether this mix of policy for deficit reduction achieves the desired results in the best way," Saxton said.
Senate Budget Chairman Pete Domenici, R-N.M., has said changes to the CPI were unlikely to be a factor in the fiscal 1998 budget, unless President Clinton and Congress together took the lead.

Representative Charles Stenholm of Texas, a leader of a group of fiscally conservative Democrats, said on Friday the group's budget again will include this year a 0.5 percent downward adjustment in the CPI to save $50 billion.
The 25 Democrats, a minority in their own party, have reached alliances with Republican moderates on some budget issues and gained considerable influence in last year's budget discussions.
The commission's report on the CPI "raised our consciousness," said Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the Labour Department's Bureau of Labour Statistics, which compiles the CPI report.
The department is making changes to the index, but "it's going to be a very long time" for all of the issues related to the inflation measure to be addressed, she said last week.
"The CPI is the best measure (of inflation) that we know how to produce at this time," Abraham said.
